1. Dataset Overview & Game Distribution

This report analyzes 20,058 completed chess games collected from Lichess.org via the platform's public API. The dataset spans casual and rated play, covers a wide spectrum of player ratings (approximately 800–2700 Elo), and includes full game metadata: player ratings, time controls, opening classifications (ECO codes), victory statuses, and move sequences.

Game Outcomes

Of the 20,058 games, 19,108 were decisive (non-draw) and 950 ended in draws (4.7%). White won 10,001 decisive games (52.34%) while Black won 9,107 (47.66%). The modest but consistent white advantage is a central theme explored in Section 2.

Figure 1.2 — How games end. Resignation is the dominant outcome (55.6%), followed by checkmate (31.5%).

Rating Distribution

The player pool is broadly representative of online chess. Mean white rating is 1,596.6 (median 1,567, SD 291.3); mean black rating is 1,588.8 (median 1,562, SD 291.0). The near-identical distributions confirm that color assignment is effectively random with respect to skill.

Figure 1.3 — Distribution of white and black player ratings. Both distributions are nearly identical, confirming random color assignment.

2. White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

The first-move advantage is the most debated empirical question in chess. In this dataset, white wins 52.34% of decisive games — a 4.7 percentage-point edge over black. While this margin appears small in absolute terms, it is highly consistent across sub-populations and grows dramatically with player strength.

Key Stat: White's win rate of 52.34% translates to an expected score of ~0.523 per game (excluding draws). In Elo terms, this is roughly equivalent to a 15–20 point rating advantage — a meaningful edge in competitive play.

White Advantage by Victory Status

White's edge is present in games ending by resignation (52.4%) and checkmate (52.9%), but vanishes in timeout situations (49.7%). This suggests that time pressure can neutralize or even reverse the initiative advantage, as black benefits from white's need to manage the clock while pressing for an advantage.

White Advantage by Rating Bracket

The most striking finding is how white's advantage scales with player strength. Among games where white is rated below 1,200, white actually loses more than wins (35.7% win rate). The advantage crosses parity in the 1,400–1,599 bracket, reaches 55.5% at 1,600–1,799, and climbs to 66.2% for 2,000+ rated players. This pattern suggests that stronger players are far more effective at converting the first-move initiative into concrete results.

Figure 2.1 — White win rate by white rating bracket. The first-move advantage is negligible at beginner levels but becomes decisive at expert level (2000+).

White Advantage by Time Control

Across the eight most common time controls, white's win rate ranges from 51.1% (10+5) to 55.3% (15+10). The advantage is relatively stable in rapid and blitz formats, with a slight uptick in longer controls that allow deeper calculation. The 15+10 control shows the largest white edge, possibly because the extra increment rewards accurate, forcing play.

Figure 2.2 — White win rate across the most popular time controls. The advantage is stable (~52%) across formats, with a modest peak at 15+10.

Interaction: Rating Bracket × Time Control

The heatmap below reveals that white's advantage is not uniform across the rating-time matrix. In the 10+0 control — the dataset's most popular format — white's win rate climbs from 38.0% (<1200) to 71.2% (2000+). The 15+15 control shows a similar trajectory. Notably, in the 1400–1,599 bracket, white outperforms across all four major time controls, suggesting this is the rating range where players first learn to exploit the initiative effectively.

Figure 2.3 — White win rate (%) heatmap by rating bracket and time control. Darker blue indicates stronger white performance.

3. Rating Dynamics and Their Impact on Outcomes

While color matters, rating differential is the single strongest predictor of game outcome. The correlation between (white_rating − black_rating) and white victory is r = 0.367 — a moderate-to-strong effect in a domain with high variance. The higher-rated player wins 64.6% of decisive games, dwarfing the first-move advantage in predictive power.

Rating Differential Distribution

The mean rating differential (white − black) is +7.8 points, with a median of +3.0 and a standard deviation of 249.0. The near-zero mean confirms random pairing; the large standard deviation reflects Lichess's open pool, where 2,900+ rating gaps are not uncommon.

Win Probability by Rating Gap

The relationship between rating differential and win probability is strikingly linear. When white is 200+ points lower-rated, white wins just 21.7% of games. At near-parity (−50 to 0), the rate is exactly 50.0%. When white enjoys a 200+ point advantage, the win rate jumps to 81.8%. This pattern validates the Elo system's theoretical predictions and demonstrates that rating is a highly reliable outcome predictor on Lichess.

Figure 3.1 — White win rate by rating differential bin. The relationship is approximately linear and validates Elo theory.

Higher-Rated Player Performance

Aggregating across both colors, the higher-rated player wins 64.6% of decisive games. This advantage is modest at small gaps (55.9% for 51–100 point differences) and overwhelming at large gaps (78.3% for 200+ point differences). The data contains no evidence of systematic rating inflation or deflation — the relationship is symmetric and monotonic.

Figure 3.2 — Higher-rated player win rate by rating differential bin. Even a 50-point gap confers a meaningful edge.

Game Length by Rating Tier

Stronger players play longer games. The average game length increases monotonically with rating tier: 52.9 turns for sub-1,400 games, 59.3 for 1,400–1,599, 63.3 for 1,600–1,799, and 67.4 for 1,800+. This trend holds across all victory statuses and suggests that stronger players defend more tenaciously, convert advantages more precisely, and avoid premature resignations.

Openings Where Black Outperforms White

Among the top 15 openings, five show a negative white win rate. The most pronounced black advantages appear in:

  • A00 (Van't Kruijs Opening) — White wins only 41.1%. This irregular opening (1.a3 or 1.h3) cedes the center and gives black easy equality.
  • B20 (Sicilian Defense: Bowdler Attack) — White wins 41.1%. The move 2.Bc4 against the Sicilian is considered passive; black scores well by challenging the bishop and seizing central space.
  • C20 (King's Pawn Game: Wayward Queen Attack) — White wins 45.7%. The early queen development (2.Qh5) is a common beginner trap that strong players punish by gaining tempi.
  • C50 (Italian Game) — White wins 47.2%. Surprisingly, this classical opening slightly favors black in this dataset. One explanation is that the sample includes many casual games where white mishandles the Giuoco Piano structure.
  • D00 (Queen's Pawn Game: Mason Attack) — White wins 48.6%. The passive 2.Bf4 setup scores below parity, suggesting that black's central control and piece activity outweigh white's slight lead in development.
Analyst Note: The negative white performance in A00 and B20 is not a statistical artifact — both have sample sizes exceeding 500 games. These openings are objectively suboptimal for white, and the data confirms that Lichess players exploit these inaccuracies effectively.

Opening Depth and Outcomes

The average opening depth is 4.8 plies (median 4). There is a modest positive correlation between opening depth and white win rate: openings lasting 5–7 plies show white win rates of 55.6%–55.7%, while ultra-short openings (1–2 plies) hover around 46–51%. This suggests that well-prepared players who steer games into known theoretical lines convert their advantage more reliably than those who deviate early.

Figure 4.2 — White win rate and game volume by opening depth (plies). Deeper opening theory correlates with stronger white performance.

5. Time Control Patterns and Game Characteristics

Time control shapes not only how games are played but how they end. The dataset is dominated by rapid chess: 10+0 alone accounts for 38.5% of all games. Blitz (5+5, 5+8) and classical (15+0, 15+15, 20+0, 30+0) make up the remainder.

Victory Status by Time Control

Checkmate rates are highest in increment formats (34.8% in 15+15) and lowest in fast blitz (28.4% in 8+0). Conversely, timeout rates peak in 8+0 (17.9%) and 10+0 (9.9%), confirming that shorter base times with no increment create acute time pressure. The 15+10 control shows the highest resignation rate (63.8%), suggesting that longer thinking time leads to more decisive positional advantages that opponents recognize and concede.

Figure 5.1 — Victory status distribution by time control. No-increment formats (8+0, 10+0) show elevated timeout rates.

Game Length by Time Control

Average game length varies from 54.1 turns (5+8) to 67.9 turns (8+0). The 8+0 outlier is driven by timeout games that extend deep into the endgame before one player flags. Classical controls (15+0, 15+10) produce moderate lengths (~60–63 turns), while increment formats tend to be slightly shorter because players use their extra time to find forcing continuations earlier.

6. Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

This section synthesizes the most actionable insights for coaches, platform analysts, and competitive players. These findings are derived directly from the 20,058-game dataset and are designed to inform decision-making without requiring a deep dive into the preceding sections.

Finding 1: The First-Move Advantage Is Real, but Rating Dominates

White wins 52.3% of decisive games — a consistent but modest edge. However, a 100-point rating differential produces a 60.8% win rate for the stronger player, an effect roughly 4× larger than color alone. For competitive players, improving one's rating is far more impactful than seeking white in tournament pairings.

Finding 2: White's Advantage Is Skill-Dependent

At sub-1,200 levels, white wins only 35.7% of games — black actually outperforms. The advantage crosses 50% at 1,400+ and reaches 66.2% at 2,000+. This implies that teaching materials emphasizing white's initiative should be targeted at intermediate and advanced players; beginners benefit more from solid defensive fundamentals regardless of color.

Finding 3: Opening Choice Matters — Some Lines Erase White's Edge

Among high-frequency openings, five show negative white performance. The Van't Kruijs Opening (A00) and Bowdler Attack (B20) are particularly damaging, with white win rates of just 41.1%. Coaches should steer students away from these passive or irregular lines. Conversely, the Philidor Defense (C41, 59.7% white WR) and Owen Defense (B00, 62.6%) are openings where white scores well — suggesting these are good teaching models for exploiting black's constrained piece play.

Finding 4: Time Controls Without Increment Produce More Timeouts and Fewer Checkmates

The 8+0 and 10+0 formats show timeout rates of 17.9% and 9.9%, respectively, compared to 3.6% in 15+15. Checkmate rates are correspondingly lower in no-increment controls. For platform designers, adding even a small increment (e.g., 2 seconds) could materially improve game quality by reducing arbitrary flagging losses and increasing the proportion of games decided by skill rather than clock management.

Finding 5: Stronger Players Play Longer, More Decisive Games

Game length increases monotonically with rating tier (52.9 to 67.4 turns), while the checkmate rate also rises. This paradox — longer games but more checkmates — reflects stronger players' ability to defend difficult positions without premature resignation, combined with superior endgame technique to deliver mate rather than winning on time or by resignation.

Finding 6: Rating Differential Follows Elo Theory Reliably

The near-linear relationship between rating gap and win probability (Figure 3.2) validates Lichess's rating system. There is no evidence of rating inflation or systematic bias in the sample. Platform analysts can use this relationship with confidence when designing matchmaking algorithms or detecting rating manipulation.

Bottom Line for Analysts: Color is a second-order effect. Rating differential, opening preparation, and time-control structure are the primary levers that determine game outcomes on Lichess. Interventions aimed at improving game quality — such as increment mandates, opening tutorials, or anti-sandbagging matchmaking — will have far greater impact than initiatives focused on balancing the first-move advantage.
